case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act’s express preemption clause bars a state-law negligent-selection claim against a freight broker for choosing an unsafe motor carrier or driver.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 49 U.S.C. § 14501(c) (FAAAA preemption clause) (including the “related to a price, route, or service of any motor carrier ... broker, or freight forwarder” language and the safety regulatory authority exception in § 14501(c)(2)(A)).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Montgomery argues that ordinary state tort claims for negligent selection (i) are not the kind of economic regulation of prices, routes, or broker services that Congress targeted in the FAAAA, (ii) at most have an attenuated/indirect effect on a broker’s services and therefore should fall outside § 14501(c)(1), and (iii) in any event fit within the statute’s safety exception because negligent-selection liability is a traditional state safety tool aimed at preventing highway injuries and deaths. Petitioner and supporting amici (States, truck-safety groups, and preemption scholars) emphasize the presumption against preemption in areas of traditional state police power, contend that reading § 14501(c) to wipe out common-law safety claims would create a regulatory vacuum (given limited federal remedies against brokers), and argue that Congress did not clearly intend to immunize brokers from generally applicable negligence standards that promote safe carrier selection.
case_analysis.respondent_position: C.H. Robinson and supporting amici argue that negligent-selection claims are expressly preempted because they directly target and reshape a broker’s core ‘service’—arranging transportation by selecting carriers—and thus ‘relate to’ broker services under the FAAAA’s broad text as construed in prior Supreme Court cases. They contend that allowing fifty different state tort standards would reintroduce the very patchwork of state-by-state regulation Congress sought to eliminate after trucking deregulation, increasing costs and altering routing/contracting practices. Respondents also argue the safety exception should be read narrowly to preserve state ‘regulatory authority’ over motor vehicles (e.g., vehicle rules, driver qualifications, insurance mandates), not to permit private damages actions that functionally regulate broker-service decisions; otherwise the exception would swallow the rule by permitting plaintiffs to repackage service-regulating claims as ‘safety’ negligence suits.
key_precedents: Morales v. Trans World Airlines, Inc., 504 U.S. 374 (1992)
American Airlines, Inc. v. Wolens, 513 U.S. 219 (1995)
Rowe v. New Hampshire Motor Transport Ass’n, 552 U.S. 364 (2008)
Dan’s City Used Cars, Inc. v. Pelkey, 569 U.S. 251 (2013)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito make the strongest point that negligent-selection liability predictably pressures a broker’s core “service,” and Morales/Rowe recognize that indirect economic pressure can suffice for preemption. But Dan’s City’s insistence that the limiting phrase “with respect to the transportation of property” must do real work counsels against reading § 14501(c)(1) to wipe out generally applicable negligence duties whose gravamen is physical highway injury rather than economic regulation of broker offerings. On the safety carveout, I remain closer to Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor: absent a clearer statement, I would not construe “safety regulatory authority … with respect to motor vehicles” so narrowly that it excludes traditional common-law duties that incentivize safe use of motor vehicles on public roads. Institutionally, a narrow rule—preserving safety-tethered negligent-selection claims while leaving Morales/Rowe preemption available where a State is effectively dictating brokers’ market-facing service terms—best fits the text, precedent, and federalism baseline.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is Dan’s City’s insistence that “with respect to the transportation of property” must limit § 14501(c)(1), but Dan’s City involved conduct collateral to transportation (post-tow storage), whereas this claim targets the broker’s core “service” of selecting a motor carrier to transport property and thus has the significant connection Morales and Rowe treat as preemptive. Justice Roberts’s concern about a “remedial vacuum” cannot justify expanding § 14501(c)(2)(A) beyond its text: “safety regulatory authority … with respect to motor vehicles” most naturally preserves direct regulation of vehicles and their operation, not a common-law damages regime that functionally re-regulates broker screening practices State by State. As Justice Alito warns, reading the safety exception to cover any suit pleaded in the name of “safety” would substantially nullify Congress’s explicit inclusion of “brokers” in the preemption clause. Nothing in my colleagues’ arguments undermines the original public meaning of the enacted language, so I would hold the negligent-selection claim preempted.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s Dan’s City point is the most substantial argument for Petitioners, but I read Dan’s City as addressing claims collateral to the transportation-arranging service; here the asserted duty and breach are the broker’s carrier-selection decision, which is the broker’s core “service” in arranging “the transportation of property,” so the limiting phrase does not take this case outside § 14501(c)(1). As Justice Barrett and Justice Gorsuch note, Morales and Rowe teach that state common-law standards can be preempted when they exert significant regulatory pressure, and negligent-selection liability predictably dictates broker screening practices in a state-by-state way Congress sought to avoid. Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on the safety exception reads “with respect to motor vehicles” too broadly; consistent with Justice Thomas’s textual point, that language most naturally preserves direct state regulation of vehicles and their operation, not an indirect damages regime that functionally re-regulates broker services. The remedial-gap concern cannot justify expanding the carveout beyond the statute’s text, especially where it would allow “safety” labeling to swallow Congress’s express inclusion of “brokers” in the preemption clause.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Thomas make the strongest textual case that negligent-selection liability targets a broker’s core “service” and that Morales/Rowe treat indirect economic pressure as enough for preemption. But Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan correctly emphasize Dan’s City’s instruction that “with respect to the transportation of property” must meaningfully limit § 14501(c)(1), and a highway-injury negligent-selection claim is not an effort to calibrate brokers’ market-facing prices, routes, or service offerings in the deregulatory sense. On the safety exception, I remain unpersuaded by Justice Barrett’s and Justice Gorsuch’s narrowing of “safety regulatory authority … with respect to motor vehicles”: common-law negligence duties aimed at preventing crashes are a traditional, core state safety tool tied to motor-vehicle risks, and Congress did not clearly eliminate that baseline remedy against brokers. The “patchwork” concern does not justify reading the statute to create sweeping tort immunity where the real-world effect is a remedial gap for severely injured motorists without a federal substitute.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s and Justice Barrett’s strongest point is that negligent-selection liability predictably pressures a broker’s core “service” of choosing carriers and, under Morales/Rowe, indirect economic effects can trigger preemption. But Dan’s City—invoked by the Chief Justice—requires that “with respect to the transportation of property” do real limiting work, and a highway-injury negligence claim is not naturally read as state regulation of market-facing broker services in the deregulatory sense Congress targeted. On the safety exception, I remain aligned with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Sotomayor that common-law negligence is a form of “safety regulatory authority,” and a duty aimed at preventing injuries from unsafe trucking is plausibly “with respect to motor vehicles” even if it operates through broker incentives. The respondents’ narrower reading (as Justice Thomas frames it) risks turning § 14501(c)(1) into broad tort immunity for traditional safety-based duties without a clearer textual statement, an implausible and unworkable statutory coherence result.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s best point is Dan’s City’s warning that “with respect to the transportation of property” must limit § 14501(c)(1), but I do not think it limits preemption here because the asserted duty targets the broker’s core transportation-arranging function—carrier selection—rather than collateral, post-transport conduct as in Dan’s City. Under Morales and Rowe, as Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett emphasize, state common-law rules are preempted when they exert significant, non-attenuated pressure on how a covered entity provides its “service,” and negligent-selection liability predictably dictates broker screening practices in a state-by-state manner. I am not persuaded by Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Sotomayor’s view that the safety exception preserves this claim: textually, “safety regulatory authority … with respect to motor vehicles” most naturally covers direct regulation of vehicles and their operation, and reading it to include damages suits against brokers would risk allowing “safety” to swallow Congress’s express inclusion of “brokers” in the preemption clause. The remedial-gap concern cannot justify expanding the exception beyond the best reading of the enacted text.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s and Justice Thomas’s strongest point is that negligent-selection liability predictably pressures a broker’s core service and, under Morales/Rowe, indirect economic effects can suffice for preemption. But Chief Justice Roberts is right to re-anchor the analysis in Dan’s City: the phrase “with respect to the transportation of property” and the separate safety carve-out must do limiting work, or else “related to” becomes a freestanding tort-immunity engine inconsistent with the statute’s structure and traditional state police powers. On the safety exception, I remain unpersuaded by Justice Barrett’s and Justice Gorsuch’s narrowing of “safety regulatory authority … with respect to motor vehicles,” because common-law negligence has long been a primary safety instrument tied to motor-vehicle risks and Congress gave no clear statement that it meant to extinguish that baseline remedy against brokers. Institutionally, the modest course is a narrow holding that preserves ordinary, safety-tethered negligent-selection claims while leaving Morales/Rowe to do their work against state economic regulation of broker services.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s best point is Dan’s City’s insistence that “with respect to the transportation of property” must limit preemption so the statute does not become a general tort-immunity provision. But Dan’s City dealt with storage/disposal conduct collateral to transportation, whereas this claim targets the broker’s carrier-selection decision—the very “service” by which a broker “arrang[es] for” the transportation of property—so Morales/Rowe’s “significant connection” and functional-pressure test is satisfied, as Justice Thomas and Justice Alito emphasize. On § 14501(c)(2)(A), I am not persuaded by the Chief Justice’s and Justice Sotomayor’s view that common-law negligent-selection falls within “safety regulatory authority … with respect to motor vehicles”; textually that clause most naturally preserves direct safety regulation of motor vehicles and their operation, not a damages regime that indirectly re-regulates broker services state-by-state. I therefore do not see a legal argument that undermines the core textual and precedential basis for preemption here.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Alito make the Respondent’s strongest point: negligent-selection liability predictably pressures a broker’s core carrier-selection “service,” and Morales/Rowe teach that even indirect economic effects can trigger preemption. But Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Dan’s City matters here because it prevents “service” + “related to” from becoming an all-purpose tort-immunity rule; the statute’s limiting language and structure—including the separate safety carveout—must do independent work. On the safety exception, I am not persuaded by Justice Thomas’s narrow reading that confines “with respect to motor vehicles” to direct equipment/operation codes, because States have long exercised “safety regulatory authority” through common-law negligence standards aimed at preventing physical injury from motor-vehicle operation, and Congress did not clearly signal an intent to preempt that baseline remedial regime. Under my pragmatic approach, the Respondent’s patchwork concern is real but cannot justify reading the exception so narrowly that it creates a consequential liability vacuum for routine highway-injury claims without a clearer statement.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 14501(c)(1) preempts state laws “related to a price, route, or service” of a broker only “with respect to the transportation of property,” a limiting phrase this Court emphasized “massively limits the scope” of FAAAA preemption. Dan’s City Used Cars, Inc. v. Pelkey, 569 U.S. 251, 261 & n.4 (2013). A generally applicable negligent-selection claim—aimed at traditional state safety responsibilities rather than economic regulation—does not “single out” broker transportation services in the way Rowe and Morales addressed, and any effect on broker services is, at most, indirect. In any event, reading § 14501(c)(2)(A)’s safety regulatory authority exception to preserve state tort duties that incentivize safe carrier selection avoids an overbroad preemption rule that would unsettle settled expectations and create an unnecessary regulatory vacuum, consistent with narrow decisionmaking and institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The FAAAA preempts any state “law, regulation, or other provision having the force and effect of law” that is “related to a price, route, or service of any … broker,” 49 U.S.C. § 14501(c)(1), and a negligent-selection claim targets the broker’s core “service” of arranging transportation by selecting a carrier. Under this Court’s broad construction of “related to” in Morales v. Trans World Airlines, Inc. and Rowe v. New Hampshire Motor Transport Ass’n, a state rule is preempted when it has a connection with or effectively dictates how transportation services are provided, even if it operates through indirect economic pressure. The safety exception in § 14501(c)(2)(A) preserves a State’s “safety regulatory authority … with respect to motor vehicles,” but that text is best read to cover direct motor-vehicle safety regulation rather than private tort suits that functionally regulate broker service decisions and recreate a patchwork Congress forbade. Because the negligent-selection claim would impose state-by-state standards on broker carrier-selection decisions, it falls within § 14501(c)(1) and outside § 14501(c)(2)(A).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 14501(c)(1) expressly preempts any state “law” or “other provision having the force and effect of law” that is “related to a price, route, or service” of a “broker,” and a negligent-selection claim squarely targets the broker’s core “service”—arranging transportation by selecting carriers—thereby pressuring brokers to alter how they provide that service. As in Rowe v. New Hampshire Motor Transport Ass’n, state requirements that effectively dictate carrier-selection and delivery arrangements are preempted even when framed as indirect regulation, because they reintroduce the patchwork Congress sought to avoid through deregulation. The safety exception in § 14501(c)(2)(A) preserves a State’s “safety regulatory authority … with respect to motor vehicles,” but a private tort suit regulating broker selection decisions is not regulation “with respect to motor vehicles” in the ordinary sense (e.g., vehicle operation standards) and reading it broadly would allow plaintiffs to circumvent § 14501(c)(1) by relabeling service-regulating claims as “safety.” Practical consequences reinforce the textual reading: allowing fifty different negligent-selection standards would function as state-by-state regulation of broker services and undermine the uniform national market Congress enacted.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 14501(c)(1) preempts only state laws "related to a price, route, or service" of a broker, and Dan’s City Used Cars, Inc. v. Pelkey instructs that Congress’s limiting phrases must be given real work to avoid overbroad preemption of state claims not aimed at transportation’s economic regulation. A negligent-selection claim targets ordinary background duties of reasonable care to prevent foreseeable highway harm, not state economic regulation of broker pricing or routing, and any effect on a broker’s "service" is at most indirect in the sense Dan’s City distinguished from claims tied to the core transportation bargain. In any event, § 14501(c)(2)(A) preserves state "safety regulatory authority" "with respect to motor vehicles," and common-law negligence actions are a traditional state safety tool to protect the public from unsafe commercial trucking practices, particularly where federal law supplies no comparable remedial scheme against brokers. Reading the preemption clause to immunize brokers from generally applicable negligence standards would undermine fairness and access to justice for injured motorists and their families without a clear statement from Congress that it meant to displace this core area of state police power.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 14501(c)(1) preempts only state laws “related to a price, route, or service” of a broker “with respect to the transportation of property,” and Dan’s City Used Cars, Inc. v. Pelkey emphasized that this limiting phrase “massively limit[s] the scope of preemption” and excludes claims whose connection to transportation services is too attenuated. A negligent-selection claim is a generally applicable background tort duty aimed at preventing physical injury, not a state rule dictating brokers’ prices, routes, or market-facing service offerings in the deregulatory sense targeted by Rowe and Morales. Even if such a claim “relates to” broker services in some indirect way, it fits comfortably within § 14501(c)(2)(A)’s safety regulatory authority exception because it is a traditional state safety tool “with respect to motor vehicles” (i.e., concerned with the risks posed by unsafe trucks and drivers on public highways). Reading the statute to wipe out this category of ordinary safety negligence suits would create an implausible immunity for broker conduct absent clearer congressional language, and Dan’s City counsels against extending preemption to claims that are “tenuous, remote, or peripheral” to the regulated economic domain.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The FAAAA expressly preempts state laws “related to a price, route, or service” of any “broker,” 49 U.S.C. § 14501(c)(1), and a negligent-selection claim targets a broker’s core “service”—arranging transportation by choosing a motor carrier—thereby exerting more than an indirect or tenuous influence on that service. Our cases read “related to” broadly to include state rules having a significant connection with covered services (Morales; Rowe), and applying fifty differing negligence standards would functionally regulate broker-service decisions in the very manner Congress sought to foreclose. Dan’s City supplies an important limiting principle, but it does so by asking whether the claim is genuinely about the transportation service at issue; here it is, because the alleged wrong is the broker’s carrier-selection decision itself rather than some collateral post-service conduct. The safety exception in § 14501(c)(2)(A) preserves state “safety regulatory authority … with respect to motor vehicles,” but textually it is aimed at direct regulation of motor vehicles and their operation, not private tort suits that recalibrate broker services nationwide under the guise of safety.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 14501(c)(1) preempts state laws “related to a price, route, or service” of a broker, but Dan’s City Used Cars, Inc. v. Pelkey stresses that statutory limiting language must be given real force and that preemption does not extend to state rules lacking a sufficiently direct connection to the preempted subject matter. A negligent-selection claim is a generally applicable state tort duty aimed at preventing highway injuries, and its impact on broker “services” is at most indirect compared to the targeted state economic regulation Congress addressed in Rowe and Morales. Even if the claim is “related to” broker services in some sense, the safety regulatory authority exception in § 14501(c)(2)(A)—“with respect to motor vehicles”—is best read, consistent with history and tradition of state police powers and workable federalism, to preserve core state safety remedies for harms arising from unsafe carrier selection. Preserving such traditional tort claims avoids an implausible immunity-by-preemption result absent a clear statement from Congress, while still leaving the FAAAA’s core deregulatory purpose intact.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 14501(c)(1) expressly preempts state laws “related to a price, route, or service of any … broker,” and a negligent-selection claim targets the broker’s core “service”—arranging transportation by selecting a carrier—thereby having the kind of significant connection this Court has treated as preempted under similarly worded clauses. See Rowe v. N.H. Motor Transp. Ass’n, 552 U.S. 364 (2008); Morales v. Trans World Airlines, Inc., 504 U.S. 374 (1992). Dan’s City confirms that Congress’s limiting phrases matter, and here the safety exception in § 14501(c)(2)(A) is textually constrained to state “safety regulatory authority … with respect to motor vehicles,” which more naturally covers direct motor-vehicle regulation rather than a private damages action that effectively regulates broker selection decisions. Reading the exception to encompass negligent-selection suits would risk swallowing the express broker preemption Congress enacted, undermining the statute’s deregulatory structure and the uniformity purpose reflected in our precedents.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 14501(c)(1) preempts state laws “related to a price, route, or service” of a broker, but this Court has cautioned that the phrase is not boundless and does not reach state claims whose link to transportation services is too remote or peripheral. Dan’s City Used Cars, Inc. v. Pelkey, 569 U.S. 251 (2013), reflects that limiting principle by rejecting preemption where the claim did not target the transportation service itself, and negligent-selection liability—aimed at preventing highway injuries—operates as a generally applicable safety tort duty rather than economic regulation of broker pricing, routing, or offerings. Even if negligent-selection has some practical effect on how brokers screen carriers, it fits comfortably within the safety regulatory authority exception in § 14501(c)(2)(A) as a traditional state safety tool “with respect to motor vehicles,” and Congress did not clearly indicate an intent to displace such core police-power remedies. Reading the clause to immunize brokers from ordinary negligence standards would create serious practical consequences—a remedial vacuum for victims—without the clear statement we ordinarily require when Congress intrudes on historic state authority over roadway safety.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 preempts a state common-law negligent-selection claim against a freight broker for choosing an unsafe motor carrier or driver.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 49 U.S.C. § 14501(c) (FAAAA preemption clause, including its exception for a State’s “safety regulatory authority” with respect to motor vehicles).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Montgomery argues that a negligent-selection claim against a broker is a traditional state tort remedy that does not regulate a broker’s “prices, routes, or services” in the deregulatory sense Congress targeted, or at most has only an indirect/attenuated effect. He further contends that even if the claim relates to broker “services,” it falls within the FAAAA’s safety exception because negligent-selection duties operate as part of the States’ historic police powers to protect highway safety and incentivize reasonable screening of carriers and drivers. Petitioner and supporting amici emphasize federalism canons (presumption against preemption in areas of traditional state authority and narrow construction of preemption clauses) and warn that broad preemption would eliminate compensation and deterrence for victims of trucking crashes while leaving no meaningful federal substitute tort remedy.
case_analysis.respondent_position: C.H. Robinson and supporting amici contend that negligent-selection claims directly target and regulate a broker’s core “service” (arranging transportation by selecting carriers) and therefore are expressly preempted because they are state “laws” (including common-law duties) “related to” broker services. Respondents argue that allowing juries to impose liability based on after-the-fact reasonableness standards would create non-uniform, state-by-state requirements on how brokers vet, hire, monitor, insure, or prioritize carriers—precisely the kind of fragmented regulation Congress sought to prevent in enacting the FAAAA. They also maintain that the safety exception is limited (focused on state regulation ‘with respect to motor vehicles’) and does not save claims aimed at broker decisionmaking or market conduct rather than direct motor-vehicle safety regulation.
key_precedents: Morales v. Trans World Airlines, Inc.
Rowe v. New Hampshire Motor Transport Ass’n
Dan’s City Used Cars, Inc. v. Pelkey

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Kagan press the best counterargument: Dan’s City requires giving real limiting effect to “with respect to the transportation of property,” and they characterize this as ordinary crash-injury law rather than economic regulation. But even taking Dan’s City seriously, this claim targets the broker’s core “service” of arranging property transportation by selecting a carrier, so under Morales and Rowe the connection is not “tenuous, remote, or peripheral” and the tort duty predictably operates as a state-by-state regulatory standard for how that service must be performed. On the safety exception, Justice Sotomayor’s police-power framing has force, yet § 14501(c)(2)(A) is textually cabined to safety authority “with respect to motor vehicles,” and a negligence rule effectively prescribing broker vetting and monitoring practices is regulation of intermediary decisionmaking, not motor vehicles in the administrable, narrowed sense Dan’s City cautions us to preserve. As Justice Alito emphasizes, allowing these claims would recreate the very patchwork of state standards Congress sought to preempt in this deregulatory scheme, and a minimalist approach counsels we adhere to that statutory design and leave any remedial gap to Congress.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Alito press the best point: negligent-selection liability can operate as de facto regulation of a broker’s core “service” and invite nonuniform state-by-state standards. But under an original public-meaning reading of § 14501(c)(1), Dan’s City’s insistence that “with respect to the transportation of property” “massively limits” the clause means we cannot treat any tort duty touching brokerage decisionmaking as sufficiently direct; a negligence claim triggered by a highway crash is too contingent and indirect to qualify as regulation of “services … with respect to the transportation of property” in the relevant sense. Justice Barrett’s and Justice Gorsuch’s narrowing of the safety exception likewise departs from the ordinary meaning of “with respect to motor vehicles,” which naturally encompasses state duties requiring reasonable care not to place unsafe motor carriers on the road. Nonuniformity and administrability concerns cannot expand preemption beyond the statute’s narrowing phrases and carveouts as originally understood.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is Dan’s City’s insistence that the limiting phrase “with respect to the transportation of property” must do real work, and that we should not treat “related to” as a roving displacement of state tort law. But this negligent-selection claim is not “tenuous, remote, or peripheral” in Dan’s City’s sense: it targets the broker’s central “service” of arranging property transportation by selecting a carrier, and under Morales and Rowe a jury-enforced common-law duty can operate as de facto regulation by dictating the diligence required for that service. Justice Thomas’s and Justice Sotomayor’s broader safety-exception reading also goes too far textually: § 14501(c)(2)(A) preserves safety authority only “with respect to motor vehicles,” and a duty aimed at broker intermediary decisionmaking (who to hire) is not regulation of motor vehicles in an administrable, narrowed way without turning the exception into a loophole for any claim with downstream safety consequences. The practical consequence Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes—nonuniform, state-by-state standards governing broker selection practices—is not mere policy gloss but confirms the statutory design Congress adopted in this deregulatory preemption scheme.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Alito’s strongest point seriously: negligent-selection liability may function as de facto regulation of a broker’s core “service” and generate nonuniform, jury-driven standards across States. But Dan’s City—invoked by Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Thomas—requires that “with respect to the transportation of property” meaningfully narrow “related to,” and a generally applicable crash-injury negligence claim is best understood as traditional safety-and-compensation law triggered by physical harm, not an economic rule about the content or pricing of brokerage services as in Morales/Rowe. On the safety exception, Justice Barrett’s administrability worry cannot justify reading “with respect to motor vehicles” so tightly that it excludes state authority to deter putting demonstrably unsafe carriers and drivers on the road; that is safety regulation in the ordinary police-power sense even when enforced through tort. Absent a clearer statement from Congress, I would not treat § 14501(c)(1) as silently displacing a core remedial mechanism for victims and a concrete deterrent to unsafe highway operations.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Alito’s strongest point is the administrability/nonuniformity concern: negligent-selection verdicts could induce state-by-state broker vetting protocols and look like de facto regulation of a broker’s core “service” under Morales/Rowe. But Dan’s City, as Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Thomas emphasize, forces us to give genuine narrowing effect to “with respect to the transportation of property,” and a negligence claim triggered by a highway crash is directed at preventing physical injury from unsafe motor-vehicle operations rather than regulating the economic content of brokerage offerings; that keeps the connection to “transportation of property” too indirect to warrant categorical preemption. On § 14501(c)(2)(A), I remain unpersuaded by Justice Barrett’s effort to confine “with respect to motor vehicles” to vehicle-focused rules: a duty of reasonable care to avoid putting an unsafe motor carrier on the road is naturally “with respect to motor vehicles,” and we should not use policy concerns about fragmentation to expand preemption beyond the statute’s textual limits. Under a pragmatic textualist approach, the workable line is to preserve traditional state safety/liability tools where the statute’s limiting phrases point us, while still preempting genuine economic regulation of broker pricing/routes/services.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s and Justice Thomas’s strongest point is Dan’s City’s insistence that “with respect to the transportation of property” genuinely narrows § 14501(c)(1), so we may not treat “related to” as boundless. But even honoring that limit, a negligent-selection claim aims at the broker’s central “service” Congress named—arranging transportation by selecting a motor carrier—so (as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett explain) the connection is direct, not “tenuous, remote, or peripheral” under Morales/Rowe, because the duty effectively prescribes the diligence required to perform that service. On the safety exception, I remain unpersuaded by Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Kagan’s police-power framing: § 14501(c)(2)(A) preserves safety authority only “with respect to motor vehicles,” and reading that to cover broker hiring/vetting decisions would erase the limiting phrase and convert downstream safety effects into an all-purpose loophole. Dan’s City thus cuts against, not for, Petitioners by instructing us to enforce limiting language on both the preemption clause and the carveout, which here points to preemption.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Alito’s strongest point is that negligent-selection liability predictably pressures brokers to adopt state-by-state vetting practices, functioning as de facto regulation of a broker’s core “service” under Morales/Rowe. But Dan’s City’s instruction—emphasized by Justice Thomas and Justice Kagan—that “with respect to the transportation of property” must “massively limit” the preemptive sweep counsels against treating a generally applicable crash-injury negligence claim as the sort of economic market regulation Congress targeted; the causal chain runs through an intervening motor-vehicle accident rather than the broker–shipper bargain itself. On § 14501(c)(2)(A), I remain unpersuaded by Justice Barrett’s and Justice Gorsuch’s narrow framing: a duty to use reasonable care not to place an unsafe motor carrier on the road is, in ordinary and traditional police-power terms, safety authority “with respect to motor vehicles,” even if enforced ex post through tort. Institutionally, I think that reading best reconciles uniformity goals with the background presumption against silently displacing core state remedies for physical injury absent clearer statutory text.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point, invoking Dan’s City, is that the limiting phrase “with respect to the transportation of property” must do genuine narrowing work and should exclude merely incidental connections. But a negligent-selection duty does not operate at the periphery; it functionally prescribes the standard of care governing the broker’s central “service” of arranging transportation by selecting a carrier, and under Morales/Rowe such jury-enforced common-law duties can amount to state regulation “related to” that service in a non-remote way. Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Kagan’s safety-focused framing is substantial, yet their reading of § 14501(c)(2)(A) risks nullifying the textual limit “with respect to motor vehicles” by extending the exception to any rule with downstream safety effects, rather than rules aimed at motor vehicles or their operation in an administrable sense. Dan’s City therefore cabins overbroad preemption, but it does not reclassify a direct regulation of broker selection practices as “tenuous” simply because the harm manifests as a crash.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito press the strongest case that negligent-selection liability will yield nonuniform, jury-driven standards that effectively dictate how brokers perform their core service, but that practical concern cannot expand § 14501(c)(1) beyond its own narrowing words. As Justice Kagan and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, Dan’s City requires “with respect to the transportation of property” to do real limiting work, and a crash-injury negligent-selection claim is principally about preventing and redressing foreseeable physical harm from unsafe highway operations, not regulating the economic features of brokerage services in the Morales/Rowe sense. On § 14501(c)(2)(A), I am not persuaded by Justice Barrett’s and Justice Gorsuch’s view that “with respect to motor vehicles” excludes a duty aimed at keeping demonstrably unsafe carriers off the road; that is safety authority in the most direct, police-power sense even if it operates through tort. Absent a clearer congressional statement or a federal remedial substitute, respondents’ broad preemption theory risks creating an accountability gap that the statute’s text does not clearly compel.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 14501(c)(1) preempts state "law[s]"—including common-law duties—that are "related to" a broker’s "prices, routes, or services," and a negligent-selection claim targets the broker’s core service of arranging transportation by choosing a carrier, much as Morales and Rowe read “related to” broadly to prevent state-by-state regulation of transportation-market practices. Dan’s City supplies the limiting principle, but it cuts against petitioner here: unlike claims merely peripheral to transportation, negligent-selection liability would functionally dictate how brokers perform carrier-selection and monitoring, creating nonuniform standards Congress sought to avoid. The § 14501(c)(2)(A) safety exception preserves state “safety regulatory authority … with respect to motor vehicles,” and under Dan’s City that phrase “massively limits” the exception to laws directly concerning motor vehicles; a broker-focused negligence duty is directed at intermediary market conduct, not regulation “with respect to motor vehicles” themselves. Given the text and our precedents favoring narrow, administrable lines that protect the deregulatory scheme’s uniformity, the claim is preempted.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 14501(c)(1) preempts only state laws "related to a price, route, or service" of a broker "with respect to the transportation of property," and that limiting phrase must be given real work under ordinary textual meaning. As Dan’s City Used Cars, Inc. v. Pelkey explained, the comparable "with respect to" language "massively limit[s]" the reach of FAAAA/ICCTA preemption; a negligent-selection tort claim for highway-collision injuries is at most an indirect effect on broker services rather than a regulation of prices, routes, or services as such. Even if the claim were deemed to relate to broker "services," it fits within § 14501(c)(2)(A)’s preserved "safety regulatory authority ... with respect to motor vehicles," because imposing a duty of reasonable care in selecting motor carriers is a safety measure tied to motor-vehicle operation on the highways. Morales and Rowe involved state measures aimed at market regulation of carrier practices, whereas this generally applicable tort duty addresses physical safety and therefore falls outside the core deregulatory target Congress identified.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 14501(c)(1) expressly preempts any state "law, regulation, or other provision having the force and effect of law"—including common-law duties—"related to" a broker’s "prices, routes, or services," and a negligent-selection claim is directed at the broker’s core service of arranging transportation by choosing carriers. Under Morales and Rowe, "related to" is construed broadly to reach state measures that have a significant connection with, or effectively dictate, how transportation services are provided, and case-by-case jury standards for vetting carriers would impose precisely the kind of nonuniform state-by-state requirements Congress sought to foreclose. The safety exception in § 14501(c)(2)(A) is limited to a State’s "safety regulatory authority … with respect to motor vehicles," and a claim aimed at broker decisionmaking about carrier selection is not regulation "with respect to motor vehicles" themselves as Dan’s City indicates in cabining preemption and savings clauses to their textual scope. Allowing such tort suits would invite an end-run around deregulation through private litigation, with predictable practical consequences for interstate transportation markets that Congress chose to prevent.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: A state negligent-selection claim seeks to vindicate traditional police-power interests in highway safety and compensation for crash victims, not to reimpose state economic regulation of brokers’ “prices, routes, or services” in the deregulatory sense Congress targeted in 49 U.S.C. § 14501(c). Under Dan’s City Used Cars, Inc. v. Pelkey, FAAAA preemption does not extend to state laws whose connection to a covered “service” is merely “tenuous, remote, or peripheral,” and negligent selection operates as a generally applicable duty of reasonable care triggered by foreseeable physical harm. Even if the claim “relates to” broker services in some sense, it fits within § 14501(c)(2)(A)’s preservation of a State’s “safety regulatory authority … with respect to motor vehicles,” because it incentivizes reasonable screening of carriers and drivers to prevent motor-vehicle crashes. Reading the statute to wipe out this core tort remedy would leave injured people without meaningful redress and would stretch Morales and Rowe beyond their focus on state measures that functioned as market regulation rather than safety-based accountability for physical injury.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 14501(c)(1) preempts state laws “related to” a broker’s “prices, routes, or services,” but our cases read “related to” to require a non-tenuous connection and to respect statutory limits, not to sweep in every background tort duty with incidental effects. Dan’s City Used Cars, Inc. v. Pelkey emphasizes that preemption does not extend to claims whose gravamen is not the provision of the transportation service itself, and a negligent-selection claim targets the broker’s failure to use reasonable care to avoid putting an unsafe motor carrier on the road—an exercise of traditional state police power over highway safety. Even if such a claim has some connection to “services,” the safety exception in § 14501(c)(2)(A) preserves state “safety regulatory authority … with respect to motor vehicles,” and a duty to avoid negligently selecting unsafe carriers is sufficiently safety-directed and workable without reimposing the kind of rate/route/service regulation condemned in Morales and Rowe. Reading the statute coherently, we should not treat Congress’s deregulatory goal as silently eliminating longstanding compensation and deterrence mechanisms in the core domain of roadway safety absent clearer text.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 14501(c)(1) expressly preempts state “law[s]” (including common-law duties) “related to a … broker’s … services,” and a negligent-selection claim targets the heart of a broker’s service—choosing and arranging a motor carrier—by inviting juries to impose state-by-state standards on that selection function. Our precedents read “related to” broadly in this context, preempting state rules that have a significant connection with or effect on carrier/broker services even if couched as general tort law. See Morales v. Trans World Airlines, Inc. and Rowe v. New Hampshire Motor Transport Ass’n. The safety exception in § 14501(c)(2)(A) is textually limited to a State’s “safety regulatory authority … with respect to motor vehicles,” and (as Dan’s City underscores about similar limiting language) that narrowing phrase constrains the carveout; a claim aimed at broker market conduct rather than direct motor-vehicle regulation does not fall within it.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 14501(c)(1) preempts state laws “related to” a broker’s “prices, routes, or services” only “with respect to the transportation of property,” a limiting phrase this Court emphasized “massively limits the scope” of FAAAA preemption. Dan’s City Used Cars, Inc. v. Pelkey, 569 U.S. 251, 261 (2013). A generally applicable state common-law negligent-selection claim is not aimed at regulating brokerage market offerings in the deregulatory sense targeted by Morales and Rowe, and its effect on broker “services” is at most indirect and contingent on particular unsafe conduct. Even if the claim is deemed to relate to “services,” it fits within § 14501(c)(2)(A)’s preservation of a State’s “safety regulatory authority … with respect to motor vehicles,” reflecting the States’ traditional police power over highway safety and providing a workable, historically grounded line that preserves both federal deregulation and core tort accountability.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 14501(c)(1) preempts any state “law” (including common-law duties) “related to” a broker’s “prices, routes, or services,” and arranging transportation by selecting a motor carrier is the broker’s core “service.” Under Rowe v. New Hampshire Motor Transport Ass’n, preemption extends beyond laws that expressly refer to services to those that have a significant effect, including indirect effects, and negligent-selection liability would predictably impose nonuniform, state-by-state standards on how brokers vet and choose carriers. The safety exception in § 14501(c)(2)(A) is textually limited to a State’s “safety regulatory authority … with respect to motor vehicles,” and a claim targeting a broker’s selection decision is not sufficiently “with respect to motor vehicles” as Dan’s City Used Cars, Inc. v. Pelkey reads that limiting phrase. Because the claim relates to broker services and does not fall within the narrow motor-vehicle-focused exception, it is expressly preempted.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 14501(c)(1) preempts state laws “related to” a broker’s “prices, routes, or services,” but this Court has cautioned against reading that phrase to sweep in claims whose connection to transportation is too attenuated; in Dan’s City Used Cars, Inc. v. Pelkey, we emphasized that statutory limiting language can “massively limit” FAAAA preemption and refused to displace state-law claims not targeting transportation services as Congress understood them. A negligent-selection claim functions as a background safety-and-compensation rule of general applicability, operating within States’ historic police powers and focused on preventing roadway harm rather than dictating brokers’ rates, routes, or offerings in the deregulatory sense addressed in Morales and Rowe. Even if such a claim has some connection to broker “services” (selection), it is best understood as falling within § 14501(c)(2)(A)’s preservation of state “safety regulatory authority … with respect to motor vehicles,” because it incentivizes reasonable screening practices that bear directly on motor-vehicle safety and has practical consequences for deterrence and victim compensation. Reading the preemption clause to eliminate this traditional tort remedy would create a serious remedial gap with no clear federal substitute, undermining procedural fairness and accountability in a core area of state responsibility.
